title: Proteostasis as an Integrating Node: Metadichol Coordinately Induces the 22-Gene HSF1/SIRT1-Anchored Chaperone Network in Human PBMCs at Picogram Concentrations
content: Background: Protein homeostasis (proteostasis) is maintained by a network of heat shock proteins (HSPs) and co-chaperones spanning the cytosol, mitochondria, and endoplasmic reticulum, under the transcriptional control of heat shock factor 1 (HSF1) and its metabolic partner SIRT1. Metadichol, a nanoemulsion of long-chain alcohols and a pan-nuclear-receptor ligand, has been reported to modulate broad gene-expression programs at very low concentrations, but its effect on the human chaperone network had not been examined directly. Methods: Human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were treated with Metadichol at 0.1 pg/mL, 1 pg/mL, 100 pg/mL, 1 ng/mL, and 100 ng/mL for 24 h. Expression of 22 HSP-network genes was quantified by SYBR Green RT-qPCR and normalized to the geometric mean of HPRT1 and RPLP0, selected by geNorm; relative expression was calculated by the 2^−ΔΔCt method. Results: Metadichol produced significant, dose-dependent up-regulation of all 22 genes. Peak fold changes ranged from 1.34× (HSPA8) to 4.00× (DNAJA3), with strong induction of the mitochondrial J-protein DNAJA3 (4.00×), the disaggregase HSPH1 (3.20×), the HSP90 co-chaperone STIP1/HOP (3.17×), the ER chaperones HSPA5/BiP (2.71×) and HSP90B1/gp96 (2.61×), and the inducible HSPA1A (2.57×). The master regulators HSF1 (1.40×) and SIRT1 (1.82×) were both induced. Responses were biphasic, with the plurality of genes peaking at 1 ng/mL and attenuating at 100 ng/mL. Genes co-varied across the dose series, indicating a coordinated rather than gene-by-gene response. Conclusions: At picogram-to-nanogram concentrations, Metadichol coordinately activates the entire HSF1/SIRT1-anchored chaperone network across all cellular compartments in primary human immune cells. This positions proteostatic capacity as a plausible integrating node linking Metadichol’s previously reported effects on nuclear receptors, reprogramming factors, and immune gene programs.
